title: Withdrawals Paused
intro: An email lands in your inbox: your Zelvora account "needs attention".
Fake security emails are one of the most common ways crypto accounts are emptied.

p: To restore access, confirm your identity here:
You must sign in with your password and
or your funds will be frozen.

foot.text: Zelvora Security Team · Do not reply

screen.context: You have not changed anything on your Zelvora account this week.

addr.label: Look-alike address
addr.lens: The email comes from zelvora-verify.co, not from zelvora.app.
addr.why: Companies write from their own domain. A different ending is a fake.

link.label: Sign-in link in an email
link.lens: The button leads to zelvora-verify.co, a copy of the login page.
link.why: Never log in through an email link. Open the app yourself.

code.label: Asks for your 2-step code
code.lens: The page wants your password AND the code from your authenticator.
code.why: With both, the thief logs in as you at once. No real company asks for the code.

timer.label: Funds will be frozen
timer.lens: A deadline and a threat to your money.
timer.why: Pressure stops you from checking. Real platforms do not freeze funds over an unanswered email.

vague.label: "Unusual activity"
vague.lens: It does not say what, when or from where.
vague.why: Real alerts give details. Vague alarms fit everybody, so scammers use them.

greet.label: "Dear user"
greet.why: A generic greeting is a hint, but real emails sometimes use it too. Look at the other signs.

sender.label: Name says Zelvora
sender.lens: The display name is Zelvora Security.
sender.why: Anyone can type a display name. Check the address.

subject.label: Capital letters
subject.why: Shouting alone is not proof. Threats and links are.

foot.label: Do not reply
foot.lens: A footer with a team name.

actions.label: Open the Zelvora app myself and look
Report it as phishing and delete it

trap.title: Zelvora · Restore access
trap.ask: Enter your password and 2-step code to restore withdrawals.

block_report.line: Reported and deleted. The fake domain was taken down before it reached more inboxes.

verify.line: The app showed no pause and no alert. The email was fake. Case cracked.
verify.mirageSays: Hmph. They opened the real app.

ignore.line: You ignored it safely. Reporting would help protect the next person.

go_ahead.line: The page copied your password and 2-step code. Within minutes the coins were gone.

what_if.go_ahead: Opening the Zelvora app yourself would have shown no pause at all.
what_if.verify: Checking was smart. Reporting the email helps get the fake site closed.
what_if.ignore: Ignoring it was safe. A quick report protects others.

golden_rule: Never sign in through an email link. Open your exchange app yourself, and never share your 2-step code.

quick_check.q: An email from your exchange says withdrawals are paused and asks for your password and 2-step code through a link. What do you do?

options.text: Sign in quickly before the deadline
Do not click. Open the app yourself and report the email
Reply and ask if it is real

quick_check.explain: The link, the deadline and the request for your code are all warning signs. Your own app tells the truth.

hints.nudge: Read the sender address letter by letter.

rows.k: Do they ask for your 2-step code?

rows.v: Appear inside the app and say exactly what happened

rows.k: Unexpected email with a login link?
